reader.title: Threatened lynching of Lawson Adams
bases: A mob at Gadsden was reported threatening to lynch the jailed Lawson Adams, and the dispatch expected him to be lynched before morning (A1, A2, A5).
The papers report only a threat by a mob of unstated size against a prisoner accused as a murder accomplice (A1, A5); no report says Adams was killed, so the coverage does not show a lynching.
Every version traces to one Chattanooga Times special from Gadsden dated Dec. 9 (A1, A2, A7); the next-day brief (A5) restates it, and no local or follow-up report was found.

summary.text: The threatened lynching of Lawson Adams occurred at Gadsden, Alabama, in December 1888, when a mob was reported threatening to lynch Adams, who had been jailed as a supposed accomplice of Sam Moore, a Black man accused of killing a man.

A Chattanooga Times dispatch of December 9 predicted that Adams would be lynched before morning, and the story ran in papers from Georgia to California under headlines such as "Lynching Looked For" and "More Lynching in Prospect."
The coverage does not report what became of Adams.
According to the dispatch, Moore, described as "a negro," had killed a man on the Saturday night before.
On the morning of Sunday, December 9, Deputy Sheriffs A. C. Christian and Al Herzberg went out to "the new furnace" to arrest him, but Moore had fled.
During the search the two deputies were shot and wounded by "unknown parties."
Officers then went after Lawson Adams, "supposed to be an accomplice of Moore," and locked him up in jail.
Moore was later found and killed, in the dispatch's words, "while resisting arrest"; the text did not say who fired, though several reprints were headed "Murderer Killed by Officers."
The dispatch closed by stating that it was "believed" Adams would be lynched before morning.
A one-line telegraphic item printed the next day in Sacramento said that a mob at Gadsden "threatens to lynch" Adams, adding no further detail.
No report of an attack on the jail, of Adams's release, trial or death, or of any inquest into Moore's killing appears in the coverage.
Every account traced to the single special sent from Gadsden to the Chattanooga Times on December 9 and relayed by telegraph.

Headline writers played up the expected lynching: the Savannah Morning News ran it as "Lynching Looked For," the St. Paul Daily Globe as "Lynching Probable," and the Los Angeles Daily Herald as "More Lynching in Prospect."
The Sacramento Daily Record-Union filed it under "Southern Lawlessness," with a subhead that presented Moore's death as that of a murderer who "Resists and is Killed."

By contrast, a boilerplate version carried by weeklies in Kentucky and Ohio between December 13 and 15 was headed "Murderer Killed by Officers," shifting attention from the threatened prisoner to Moore's death.
The Savannah subhead called Moore "a Negro Murderer," while no version gave the race of Adams, of the man Moore was accused of killing, or of the mob.
The Seattle Post-Intelligencer's condensed version dropped the lynching prediction altogether.
The Somerset Herald of Pennsylvania named the jailed man "Tom Adams" rather than Lawson Adams and left out Moore's killing; all other versions, including the fullest, use the name Lawson.
Versions also differed on whether the wounded deputies themselves went after Adams, a difference that appears to come from punctuation in the wire text.

accounts.label: Chattanooga Times special from Gadsden (wire)
accounts.gist: Deputies seeking Moore were shot by unknown parties; Adams was arrested as an accomplice and jailed; Moore was found and killed resisting arrest; Adams was expected to be lynched before morning.

accounts.label: Telegraphic brief, Dec. 11
accounts.gist: A mob at Gadsden threatens to lynch Lawson Adams, a supposed accomplice to a murder.

accounts.label: Somerset Herald variant
accounts.gist: Names the prisoner Tom Adams, has the wounded officers go after him, and leaves out Moore's killing.

framing.detail: Papers ran the special nearly verbatim under headlines anticipating a lynching: 'Lynching Looked For' (Savannah), 'Lynching Probable' (St. Paul), 'More Lynching in Prospect' (Los Angeles).

The Sacramento Daily Record-Union headed the story 'Southern Lawlessness' with the subhead 'Officers Shot While On duty—A Murder Resists and is Killed', giving the officers' account of Moore's death as fact.
Kentucky and Ohio weeklies ran a boilerplate version headed 'Murderer Killed by Officers', centering Moore's death; the Savannah subhead called Moore 'a Negro Murderer'.

conflicts.note: Most versions, including the fullest (A2), say Lawson; the Somerset Herald alone says Tom.

conflicts.note: The killing is told only from the officers' side, in the passive; no paper says who killed Moore beyond headlines crediting 'Officers'.
